title: SLAs, priorities and escalation
monthTitle: The Helpdesk Professional: ITIL, Ticketing & Soft Skills
summary: Understand how SLAs, impact and urgency set a ticket's priority, and learn to escalate cleanly so the right people get the right tickets at the right time.
objectives: Explain what a Service Level Agreement (SLA) is and what it commits to
Calculate priority from impact and urgency using a priority matrix
Distinguish response time targets from resolution time targets
Recognise a major incident and how it is handled differently
Escalate functionally and hierarchically with a complete handover
Prioritise a realistic mixed queue of tickets correctly

quiz.q: What is a Service Level Agreement (SLA)?
options: A documented commitment to respond and resolve within agreed timeframes
quiz.why: An SLA is an agreement between IT and the business defining target response and resolution times, often varying by priority.

quiz.q: How is a ticket's priority normally determined?
quiz.why: Priority comes from a matrix of impact (how many/how critical) and urgency (how time-sensitive), giving a consistent, defensible ranking.

quiz.q: Which scenario is most likely a P1 / major incident?
options: One user wants a larger monitor
The company email system is down for everyone
quiz.why: High impact (everyone) plus high urgency (core service down) makes an organisation-wide email outage a top-priority/major incident.

quiz.q: What is the difference between functional and hierarchical escalation?
options: Functional sends it to a team with the right skills; hierarchical raises it to management for authority or attention
quiz.why: Functional escalation routes to specialists by skill; hierarchical escalation raises the ticket up the management chain, often for SLA breaches or major incidents.

quiz.q: Explain the difference between an SLA response time and a resolution time.
quiz.answer: Response time is how quickly someone must acknowledge or begin work on the ticket; resolution time is how long is allowed to actually fix it. Both are usually set per priority.
quiz.why: Response and resolution are separate clocks; you can meet a response target but still breach the resolution target if the fix runs long.

quiz.q: What information must you include when escalating a ticket to keep it clean?
quiz.answer: The ticket reference, a clear summary of the issue, what you already tried and ruled out, the impact and priority, and the user's contact details, so the next team can continue without re-interviewing the user.
quiz.why: A complete handover prevents wasted time and a frustrated user repeating themselves; incomplete escalations bounce back.

body_markdown:
## What an SLA actually promises

A **Service Level Agreement (SLA)** is a documented promise between IT and the business about how fast tickets will be handled. It usually sets two separate clocks per priority: a **response time** (how quickly someone acknowledges and starts work) and a **resolution time** (how long is allowed to fix it). When a ticket exceeds its target, that is an **SLA breach** — something the desk works hard to avoid.

```text
Priority  Response target   Resolution target
P1        15 minutes        4 hours
P2        30 minutes        8 hours
P3        4 hours           2 business days
P4        1 business day    5 business days
```

The SLA is why you cannot just work tickets in the order they arrive — some have a much tighter clock than others.

## Priority = impact x urgency

Priority is not about who complains loudest. It is calculated from **impact** (how many people, how critical the service) and **urgency** (how time-sensitive). Most desks use a **priority matrix**:

```text
              Urgency High   Urgency Med   Urgency Low
Impact High      P1            P2            P3
Impact Med       P2            P3            P4
Impact Low       P3            P4            P4
```

A single user who forgot a password is high urgency *to them* but low impact, so it is not a P1. The whole sales floor losing email is high impact *and* high urgency — that is a **P1**.

## Major incidents

A **major incident** is the most severe class: a critical service down, many users affected, the business hurting. These get special handling — a **major incident manager**, a dedicated bridge call, frequent communications, and all-hands focus. As Tier 1, your role is often to **recognise** one early, log it correctly, and raise the alarm rather than quietly working it alone.

## Escalation done well

No single technician can fix everything, so **escalation** is a normal, healthy part of the job. There are two kinds:

- **Functional escalation** — sending the ticket to a team with the right **skills** (e.g. networking).
- **Hierarchical escalation** — raising it up the **management** chain for authority or attention, common on SLA breaches and major incidents.

A clean escalation is a complete **handover**. Bad escalations bounce back and waste everyone's time:

```text
Escalation note:
Ref: INC0048213 | Priority: P2
Summary: Finance shared mailbox not receiving external email since 08:30.
Tried: confirmed mailbox exists, internal mail arrives, checked rules
       (none blocking), verified user permissions OK.
Impact: 6 finance users, month-end deadline today.
Contact: Sam Patel, ext. 4471, available until 17:00.
Reason for escalation: needs mail-flow/transport rule review (Tier 2).
```

That handover lets the next team start immediately, without re-interviewing the user.

## Your task

You have these four tickets open at once. Assign each a priority (P1-P4) using impact and urgency, then list the order you would work them and write one sentence justifying each:

1. The entire warehouse cannot scan stock; shipping is halted.
2. One user's mouse scroll wheel is sticky.
3. A manager cannot open a report needed for a board meeting in one hour.
4. The shared printer on floor 2 is out of toner (a spare is in the cupboard).

slides.narration: Welcome back. On a busy service desk you'll never have just one ticket; you'll have a queue. So how do you decide what to work first, and when to hand something off? This lesson covers the three ideas that answer that: service level agreements, how priority is calculated from impact and urgency, and how to escalate cleanly. Master these and your queue stops feeling like chaos and starts feeling like a system.

slides.narration: First, the service level agreement, or SLA. It's a documented promise between IT and the business about how fast tickets get handled. It sets two separate clocks per priority. A response time, which is how quickly someone acknowledges and starts work, and a resolution time, which is how long is allowed to actually fix it. If a ticket goes past its target, that's an SLA breach, and the desk works hard to avoid those. This is exactly why you can't just work tickets in arrival order.

slides.title: Priority = impact x urgency
bullets: Not about who complains loudest.

Urgency: how time-sensitive.
A matrix gives a consistent ranking.
slides.code:
Urg High  Urg Med  Urg Low
Impact High     P1        P2       P3

slides.narration: So how is priority decided? Not by who complains loudest. It's calculated from two factors: impact, meaning how many people and how critical the service, and urgency, meaning how time-sensitive it is. Most desks use a priority matrix like this one. You find the impact row and the urgency column, and where they meet is your priority. It's consistent, it's fair, and crucially, it's defensible when someone insists their issue is the most important one.

slides.title: Worked example
bullets: Forgotten password: urgent to them, low impact.
So it's not a P1.
Whole floor loses email: high impact and urgency.
That's a P1.
slides.narration: Let's work an example. A single user who forgot their password feels very urgent to them, but the impact is low, it affects just one person, so it isn't a P1. Now compare: the entire sales floor loses email. That's high impact, lots of people, and high urgency, a core service is down. That combination lands squarely on P1. See how the matrix keeps you objective? You're judging the business effect, not the volume of the complaint.

slides.title: Major incidents
bullets: The most severe class: critical service down.
Many users, business actively hurting.
Special handling: manager, bridge call, comms.
Your job: recognise and raise it early.
slides.narration: At the very top sits the major incident. This is the most severe class: a critical service is down, many users are affected, and the business is actively hurting. Major incidents get special handling, a dedicated major incident manager, a bridge call, frequent communications, and all-hands focus. As a Tier one technician, your key role is often to recognise one early, log it correctly, and raise the alarm, rather than quietly trying to work it alone at your desk.

slides.title: Two kinds of escalation
bullets: Escalation is normal and healthy.
Functional: send to a team with the skills.
Hierarchical: raise up the management chain.
Hierarchical is common on breaches.
slides.narration: No single technician can fix everything, so escalation is a normal, healthy part of the job, not a sign of failure. There are two kinds. Functional escalation sends the ticket to a team with the right skills, like networking. Hierarchical escalation raises it up the management chain for authority or attention, which is common on SLA breaches and major incidents. Knowing which kind you need, skills or authority, helps you escalate to exactly the right place the first time.

slides.title: A clean handover
bullets: Include the ticket reference and priority.
Summarise the issue and the impact.
State what you tried and ruled out.
Give the user's contact details.
slides.code:
Ref: INC0048213 | P2
Summary: Finance mailbox no external mail since 08:30.
Tried: mailbox exists, internal mail OK, rules checked.
Impact: 6 users, month-end today. Contact: Sam x4471.
slides.narration: When you do escalate, make it a clean handover. A good escalation note includes the ticket reference and priority, a clear summary, the impact, what you already tried and ruled out, and the user's contact details. Look at the example: the next team can start work immediately, without re-interviewing the user. Bad escalations, the vague one-liners, just bounce straight back and waste everyone's time, especially the user's, who has to explain it all over again.

slides.title: Working the queue
bullets: Highest priority first, watch the clock.
Balance SLA risk across tickets.
Keep lower-priority users informed too.
Escalate before you breach, not after.
slides.narration: Putting it together, here's how you work a real queue. Generally you take the highest priority first, while keeping an eye on which tickets are closest to breaching their SLA clock. You balance that risk across everything you hold. And don't forget the lower-priority users, keep them informed so they're not left in silence. One more pro tip: escalate before you breach, not after. Raising your hand early is always better than missing the target quietly.

slides.title: Recap & your task
bullets: SLAs set response and resolution clocks.
Priority comes from impact and urgency.
Major incidents get special handling.
Escalate cleanly with a full handover.
Task: prioritise and order four tickets.
slides.narration: Let's recap. SLAs set two clocks, response and resolution, per priority. Priority itself comes from impact times urgency, read off a matrix. The most severe cases are major incidents with special handling. And escalation, whether functional or hierarchical, must be a clean, complete handover. Your task: take the four tickets on the page, assign each a priority from P1 to P4, then list the order you'd work them with one sentence of justification each. See you in the next lesson.
